# The Architect's Role {#sec-what-architect-owns}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Everyone designs who devises courses of action aimed at changing existing situations into preferred ones."*
>
> — Herbert A. Simon, *The Sciences of the Artificial* (1969) [@Simon1969SciencesArtificial]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note.** Herbert Simon defined design through the course from a
present situation to a preferred one. The definition places problem choice,
abstraction, boundaries, and product tradeoffs inside the technical work.
Automation can contribute substantially, but responsibility follows from
choosing and defending that course rather than replacing the work.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
Given the bounded assessment from @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect, and even
if AI can perform substantial design work, what do architects and
organizations still contribute and remain responsible for?
:::

The bounded complete-system assessment from
@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect is not permission to act. It reports what
the assessed system achieved, what it cost, where the result held, and how the
system failed. This finale begins where that assessment stops.

Grant the strongest premise in this book. AI systems can help formulate a
study, propose mechanisms, generate artifacts, search a large design space,
operate tools, interpret failures, and prepare a technical recommendation.
Nothing in this chapter depends on preserving a small protected set of tasks
that only people can perform.

The actual Lighthouse record remains bounded. @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect
reports three unresolved results. The implementation-facing architecture
outcome is unresolved, the incremental contribution of AI is unresolved, and
the moonshot program test is unresolved. The implementation study has not run
across the workload, software, interface, memory, energy, security, and
physical conditions required to freeze the array and its interface. The
matched, repeated comparison needed to assess AI contribution is also
incomplete.

This finale must hold both facts at once. AI can perform substantial technical
work, and the current architecture record does not support commitment. The
architect's role is not whatever work automation has failed to absorb. It is
the technical judgment that decides what problem should be solved, which
abstractions and boundaries are valid, how cross-layer consequences should be
composed, and whether the resulting evidence and residual risk justify a
commitment.

Two boundaries organize the finale. The quality and scope of the supporting
results determine what an architect may conclude. Assigned authority
determines who may act on that conclusion. Strong support does not grant
permission, and authority does not strengthen a weak result. Judgment,
action rights, capacity, residual risk, transfer, and reopening must keep both
boundaries visible.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Separate the AI program assessment from the architecture commitment and
  explain why neither result determines the other.
- Identify the architect's positive technical contribution in problem
  framing, abstraction, boundaries, missing constraints, cross-layer
  tradeoffs, mechanism, and consequence.
- Assign proposal, execution, acceptance, rejection, waiver, commitment,
  monitoring, containment, and reopening rights to roles with the authority
  and capacity to exercise them.
- Decide whether residual risk has a valid mitigation, containment path,
  owner, expiration, and reopening condition.
- Close the Lighthouse with a concrete architecture action and continuing
  responsibility rather than another process checklist.
:::

## Two Independent Decisions

The assessment and commitment answer different questions. The program
assessment asks whether the complete AI-assisted system improved architecture
work over a credible alternative at acceptable total cost. The architecture
commitment asks whether this design, under this problem framing, abstraction,
system boundary, evidence limit, organizational capacity, and residual risk,
should advance.

@tbl-two-closing-decisions shows why none of the three program statuses
determines the architecture action.

| **Program assessment** | **What it means for architecture commitment** |
| --- | --- |
| Supported | AI improved the architecture by at least the declared minimum worthwhile margin within the acceptable total-cost envelope, or reduced total cost by at least the declared margin while architecture quality remained within the noninferiority margin. The architecture may still be refused because the design, evidence, capacity, or residual risk is unacceptable. |
| Unsupported | AI did not show the required incremental benefit. A sound architecture may still be committed on evidence produced by a conventional or human-directed workflow. |
| Unresolved | No AI-contribution claim is justified. The architecture may proceed only if independent design evidence supports it, or it may remain uncommitted while missing work is completed. |

: **Capability assessment and architecture commitment remain independent.**
A favorable result on one cannot substitute for a favorable result on the
other. {#tbl-two-closing-decisions tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

Reviewability supports both decisions and replaces neither. A well-documented
study can still show that AI added no value. A reviewable design can still be
too risky to commit. Conversely, a useful architecture is not evidence that AI
improved the process that produced it.

The current Lighthouse state makes the separation concrete. Its AI program
assessment is unresolved. Its implementation evidence is also unresolved. The
missing implementation evidence requires refusal of the current
array-and-interface freeze. The unresolved program assessment independently
prevents a claim that AI improved the work. The freeze refusal is not a
permanent rejection of the 32 by 32 candidate or the moonshot. The reference
candidate remains available for the bounded implementation-readiness study.

## The Architect's Technical Contribution

Architects do not enter only after a search finishes. Architecture begins
before the candidate set exists and continues after a local result looks
clean. The technical contribution lies in deciding what the system is, which
relationships matter, and which consequences the study must expose.

The judgments in @tbl-architect-technical-judgments cannot be reduced to a
signature. They can be informed by models, tools, and specialists, and they
may be distributed across an authorized architecture team.

| **Judgment** | **Architectural question** | **Lighthouse consequence** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Problem choice and reframing | Is the stated problem still the one the product needs solved? | The task is not merely to maximize array utilization. It is to decide whether an implementation-facing compute and software interface meets the mobile XR obligation. |
| Abstraction | Which details can be simplified for this decision, and which must remain visible? | A cycle-level array model can compare mappings locally, but it cannot hide compiler behavior, memory traffic, physical timing, or the 3\ W subsystem boundary from a freeze decision. |
| System boundary | Where do workload, software, hardware, package, physical design, and product effects meet? | Array dimensions and dataflow cannot be separated from the runtime, interconnect, memory, energy, and implementation path they require. |
| Missing constraints | What has the formulation, representation, objective, or tool path left out? | Representative workloads, interface cost, subsystem power, implementation feasibility, security properties, and containment remain open obligations. |
| Cross-layer tradeoff | Which feasible point best serves the product when objectives conflict? | Performance, energy, programmability, reversibility, schedule, and review burden must be composed rather than delegated to separate optimizers. |
| Mechanism and consequence | Does the proposed explanation fit the observations, and what happens if it is wrong? | The failed directional shape-and-mapping explanation cannot support transfer. A wrong freeze could harden a poor software contract and create costly RTL and physical rework. |
| Commitment under uncertainty | Are the remaining risks understood, containable, and worth accepting with the available organizational capacity? | The missing implementation-facing tests block the current freeze. The absent matched comparison independently leaves the AI program test unresolved. |

: **Architecture judgment gives technical work its system meaning.** The
architect chooses the question, abstraction, boundary, and consequence before
deciding whether to commit. {#tbl-architect-technical-judgments tbl-colwidths="[20,38,42]"}

### Choosing Across Layers

Search can find useful candidates and approximate a tradeoff frontier.
Choosing a point on that frontier is a different act. A wider network link may
improve camera-ingest latency while raising switching activity and routing
pressure. A narrower link may save dynamic power while increasing queueing or
software scheduling sensitivity. Some designs may improve both objectives
before the true tradeoff appears. The architect does not assume conflict in
advance. The architect determines which objectives, constraints, operating
conditions, and product consequences make one feasible point preferable to
another.

Finding the frontier is a search problem. Choosing a point on it commits the
product. That choice includes effects that no one optimizer may represent,
such as software turnover, difficult-to-reverse interfaces, verification
capacity, package constraints, field containment, or a user-experience
threshold. A weighted objective can encode a declared tradeoff, but it cannot
decide whether the weights still represent the product.

The architecture role composes specialist judgments rather than replacing
them. A compiler lead may own whether a lowering path supports an instruction.
A verification lead may own whether a property passed within its stated
scope. A physical-design lead may own timing, power delivery, or routing
results. A product authority may own a workload or battery obligation. The
architectural contribution is to determine whether those results address one
coherent system decision and whether any interface between them remains
unowned.

### Making Missing Constraints Reviewable

Some of the most important constraints first appear as expert judgment rather
than a field in a schema. A compiler specialist may know that a proposed
instruction has no efficient lowering in the supported toolchain. A physical
designer may recognize that a placement heuristic is unsafe for a particular
power-grid geometry, bump pattern, simultaneous-current profile, and
decoupling plan. A product architect may know that a small tail-latency change
crosses a visible XR threshold even when average performance improves.

AI can help locate, compare, and organize these judgments. It cannot make them
authoritative merely by writing them down. The pattern in
@fig-tacit-extraction-bridge keeps validation between elicitation and project
state.

![**Reviewing domain knowledge before using it.** A model can help elicit and organize domain knowledge, but a named domain expert must validate constraints, assumptions, and rejection conditions. Conflicts, expiration, or new evidence require another review rather than a silent overwrite.](images/F11b-tacit-extraction-bridge){#fig-tacit-extraction-bridge width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram showing domain knowledge passing through AI-assisted elicitation and domain validation before entering represented study state, with conflict, expiration, and new evidence returning the record for revalidation."}

Read the figure from left to right. Situated domain knowledge enters a
model-assisted elicitation step that can organize documents, interview
material, assumptions, and contradictions. A named domain expert then
challenges each proposed entry and approves, rejects, or qualifies it. Only
the validated portion enters the represented study state as a constraint,
assumption, rejection check, or validity condition. The blocked direct path
makes the authority boundary explicit, while the return path sends conflicts,
expired conditions, and new evidence back for revalidation. Elicitation can
make a judgment inspectable, but it cannot make the judgment authoritative.

Consider a senior physical designer's rule against placing two high-current
macros on the same power stripe. The geometry and peak-current basis become
project state, the applicable current threshold becomes an environment
constraint, and a floorplan check can reject a violating candidate. The
designer may still need to judge which macros justify the routing cost of
separation. Every retained part needs its source, scope, owner, and
revalidation condition. A change to the power-grid template must reopen the
rule rather than leave it in force as timeless expertise.

### Judging Mechanism and Consequence

An architecture result can be numerically correct while its explanation is
wrong. @sec-running-the-loop produced a local no-change outcome and a failed
mechanism explanation. The architect preserves both. The score constrains the
local candidate ranking and technical recommendation under the tested
conditions. The failed explanation blocks transfer based on that mechanism.

This distinction matters because commitment extends beyond the measured
quantity. A mechanism supports predictions about changed workloads, software,
interfaces, or implementation. When it fails, the architect must narrow the
claim, request a discriminating test, or refuse the transition that depends on
it. Fluency, agreement among components, or a clean trajectory does not repair
the missing causal support.

Two automated reviewers may share a common source, model family, retrieval
path, or specification error. Their agreement can corroborate a result without
constituting an independent check. A materially different observation path or
instrument, together with knowledge of correlated failures where available,
is what reduces the shared assumption. The architect decides whether the
remaining dependence is acceptable for the action under review.

## Assigning Rights to Actions

Work is delegated when a person, tool, or AI system is permitted to perform
it. Responsibility is assigned when a named role must set the governing
conditions, judge the result, authorize the action, and answer for what
follows. The architecture role may be distributed across a team or review
body. It should not be disguised as one heroic person or one ceremonial
signature.

The study can delegate work broadly without delegating the basis for a claim
or the authority for an action. @fig-architect-owned-boundary makes those
relationships visible across the same study.

![**Delegated work and assigned responsibility.** Within a defined study, models, tools, checks, and specialists may assist with problem framing, representation, method choice, tool work, result interpretation, and decision preparation. Named roles remain responsible for scope, abstraction, evidence standards, automation authority, exceptions and waivers, final approval, ownership transfer, and reopening.](images/F11a-architect-owned-boundary){#fig-architect-owned-boundary width="100%" fig-alt="Architecture study containing several kinds of delegated assistance, an architectural claim for review, supporting instruments, and a full-width band of assigned responsibilities."}

Read the figure from top to bottom. The upper region places AI systems, tools,
and specialists across the architecture capabilities the study requires, from
framing through decision preparation. The center makes the architectural
claim the unit of review and binds it to a proposition, scope, evidence,
counterevidence, and qualification. Comparisons, checks, replay, iteration, and
the study record support that review without becoming the decision owner. The
lower band keeps scope, abstraction, evidence standards, automation limits,
exceptions, final decisions, transfer, and reopening assigned across the
entire study. Delegation can therefore expand without letting either the
supported claim or the responsible action disappear between components.

Execution, acceptance, rejection, waiver, commitment, and reopening are
different rights. Permission to run a tool does not grant permission to accept
its result. Permission to reject a candidate does not grant permission to
waive the failed check. A system under evaluation may propose a change to a
constraint or test, but it may not silently alter the conditions by which it
is judged. An independent owner must validate the proposed change.

The Lighthouse assignments in @tbl-lighthouse-action-rights make these rights
concrete. Role names denote responsible functions. A role may authorize a
method or tool-connected system to perform work without transferring the
authority for the action. An organization may assign one person to several
roles only when that person has the required authority, capacity, and
independence.

Consider a coherence verifier that returns a counterexample against a declared
blocking property. The verification owner may veto that candidate within the
property's stated scope. The proposing system may not weaken the property,
remove the failing workload, or redefine the counterexample as a pass. If the
verification and software owners disagree about whether the property matches
the product contract, the disagreement escalates to the system architecture
role and the authorized review authority with both domain judgments attached.
Only the role authorized to set that acceptance criterion may change it, and
the change creates a new basis that must be checked. It does not retroactively
turn the failed result into support.

| **Action** | **Responsible role** | **Required capacity and boundary** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Propose and screen candidates | Method owner and domain engineers | May authorize the study system to act inside the declared design space and budget; cannot accept a candidate or edit evaluator-owned checks. |
| Execute tools and retain returns | Environment owner | May authorize the study system to invoke tools; must preserve candidate identity, tool conditions, failures, cost, access limits, and the ability to stop. |
| Accept a bounded technical result | Relevant workload, software, verification, performance, physical, power, security, or reliability owner | Possess the expertise and access to challenge the check; acceptance remains limited to that technical scope. |
| Reject a candidate | Any owner of a declared blocking requirement in their scope | Cite the failed requirement and returned result; rejection needs no permission from the proposer. |
| Waive a failed requirement | Designated exception authority with concurrence from the affected domain owner and product-risk owner | State scope, consequence, uncertainty, mitigation, containment, expiration, and reopening trigger. No waiver may rewrite the program assessment. |
| Recommend an architecture action | System architecture role | Compose the cross-layer results, alternatives, dissent, evidence limits, total cost, and residual risk. |
| Freeze an interface or commit the architecture | Authorized architecture or product review authority with all required technical concurrences | Confirm owner capacity, accepted residual risks, mitigation, containment, and the conditions that reopen the decision. |
| Sign off and release for tapeout | Assigned signoff and release authorities | Complete the required domain signoffs and release process. No single generic “architect signature” substitutes for them. |
| Monitor, contain, reopen, repair, or retire | Named lifecycle, incident, product, and architecture roles | Possess the telemetry, access, mitigation levers, escalation path, and authority needed after the original decision. |

: **Rights attach to actions, not to a level of automation.** Every
consequential action has a scope, authorized role, capacity requirement, and
path for challenge or reopening. {#tbl-lighthouse-action-rights tbl-colwidths="[22,28,50]"}

### A Signature Is Not a Capacity Check

Naming an owner does not establish ownership in practice. The role must have
the authority to stop or redirect the work, technical competence to recognize
the relevant failure, access to the underlying artifacts and tools, time to
perform the review, and an escalation or mitigation path that can still change
the outcome. A person held answerable without these conditions becomes a
blame-absorbing role rather than an effective owner
[@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones].

Capacity is action-specific. A compiler specialist may be fully capable of
accepting a lowering result and incapable of accepting a power-delivery risk.
A product authority may have the right to commit the product and still require
concurrence from timing, verification, safety, or security roles. A review
body can distribute work, but it must not leave an interface where every role
assumes another owns the consequence.

Automation bias can remain even when the assigned reviewer is qualified
[@SkitkaEtAl1999AutomationBias]. One useful review design is to have the
reviewer form an initial position from the underlying results before seeing
the automated recommendation. This is a proposed independence measure, not a
guarantee. Its value should be tested against the actual review task and error
pattern.

Capacity can also erode when automation removes the practice that once
developed it. Bainbridge described this as an irony of automation. The person
left to handle an unusual failure may have had the routine work needed to learn
the system removed [@Bainbridge1983Ironies]. In architecture, routine practice
can expose tool behavior, cross-layer failure signatures, and the assumptions
a clean check can miss. Delegating every ordinary mapping, timing review, or
physical-design diagnosis can therefore weaken the independent challenge path
even when the formal assignment remains unchanged.

Direct practice is part of challenge capacity, not a claim that routine work
must remain manual. Roles authorized to accept, waive, or commit consequential
results need enough continuing contact with tools, failures, and cross-layer
effects to recognize when automation has left its supported scope. The purpose
is to preserve an exercisable challenge path, not to reserve work for people
merely because it was once manual.

The capacity test is direct. Could the named role, with its real authority,
access, expertise, time, and review volume, have detected the failure and
stopped or contained the action? If not, the assignment is incomplete.

## Deciding Residual Risk and Containment

Commitment does not mean that every uncertainty disappeared. It means an
authorized organization decided which remaining risks it could accept, which
it would mitigate, and which blocked the action. Residual risk is therefore a
technical and product decision, not a blank field filled after the design has
already advanced.

A usable residual-risk statement binds the failure mode, affected scope,
consequence, and basis of uncertainty to an owner and the required
concurrences. It states the likelihood and exposure when they can be estimated,
and says when they cannot. It also names the mitigation and its validating
check, the containment or rollback action, the response signal, and the
expiration or reopening condition. Rejected alternatives and unresolved
dissent remain attached so that later reviewers can distinguish accepted risk
from a missing analysis.

The waiver is the narrowest form of this decision because it permits progress
despite a failed or incomplete requirement. It must name the exact candidate,
condition, and check it covers. It must not become a blanket exception or
silently alter the acceptance criteria.

Consider a hypothetical optional Lighthouse vector-turbo mode whose subsystem
power and thermal behavior remain insufficiently characterized. Retaining the
circuitry for later study does not justify enabling the mode. A defensible
exception would require a verified disabled state, an enable path restricted
to an authorized lab or privileged service mode, verified reset, fault, and
access-control behavior, proof that the disabled circuitry does not violate
the base design's functional, timing, power, or security requirements, a named
owner, and an expiration tied to post-silicon characterization. If the
disabled state, isolation, or restricted enable path cannot be validated, the
feature is removed or the design does not advance. The exception does not turn
missing evidence into a pass. At expiration, a new decision must authorize
enablement from new evidence, renew a narrower exception, keep the mode
permanently disabled, or remove it.

Repeated exceptions can normalize a known failure until it looks like the
baseline, the organizational pattern Diane Vaughan described as normalization
of deviance [@Vaughan1996Challenger]. Expiration and reopening prevent a
temporary decision from becoming permanent merely because the system stops
reporting it.

### Design Containment Before Commitment

Containment authority matters only when the design contains a credible
technical lever. Depending on the failure, that lever may be a verified
feature-disable path, safe firmware fallback, derating mode, redundant
resource, isolation boundary, rollback path, or refusal to expose the
capability. Some failures have no safe containment short of repair or
replacement. The absence of a credible lever is itself a reason to refuse a
difficult-to-reverse commitment.

Disable mechanisms are not universal insurance. The disabled state must be
verified, the failure must be isolated from required behavior, and the control
path must remain available under the fault being contained. Errata and later
steppings provide established channels for describing and repairing some
silicon defects, but not every erratum has a workaround and not every later
revision fixes it.[^fn-errata-stepping-c11]

[^fn-errata-stepping-c11]: An erratum records a design defect or error that may
cause released silicon to deviate from published specifications, and it may
include a workaround when one exists. A stepping is a revised implementation
of a product. Either can help manage a defect, but neither guarantees
containment or repair
[@Intel2014CoreMIOUpdate].

## Testing Organizational Capacity

An individual assignment sits inside an organization that must make the right
exercisable over time. The commitment should stop when the organization lacks
the capacity to inspect, challenge, contain, or reopen a material part of the
decision.

That capacity has three parts. The decision basis must remain locatable,
including the question, candidate, conditions, results, alternatives,
exceptions, dissent, and current status. Authorized reviewers need the
technical access, independence, expertise, time, and manageable volume required
to challenge their assigned claims. The organization must also be able to stop
the workflow, contain a committed feature where technically possible, fund
repair or retirement, and transfer open obligations without losing their
scope or reopening conditions. A gap in any part makes the corresponding right
nominal rather than exercisable.

Opaque external dependencies do not make responsibility disappear. A design
may depend on a vendor model, licensed IP, an access-restricted process design
kit, and a commercial tool that the integrating team cannot inspect fully.
The committing organization should record the authorized inputs, versions,
licenses, provider attestations, observable checks, contractual allocation,
and failures that would remain difficult to diagnose. It cannot prove the
contents of an unavailable training corpus or promise exact replay after a
vendor service changes. Those limits become residual risk in the commitment
rather than invisible assumptions.

The organization retains responsibility for its architecture commitment even
when engineering work and contractual or legal obligations are distributed
across suppliers. The appropriate release authority and liability depend on
the product, contracts, jurisdiction, and regulatory context. This chapter
assigns the technical decision; it does not replace those regimes.

## Transferring and Continuing Responsibility

Ownership transfer is the transfer of an argument rather than just a report.
The next role needs enough context to understand what was decided, why the
evidence supported that action, which alternatives failed, what was waived,
and which later condition can overturn the result.
@tbl-ownership-transfer names the minimum parts of that argument.

| **Transfer object** | **What must travel** | **Failure if omitted** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decision and scope | Architecture question, workload, objective, boundary, candidate, action, and status | The new owner repeats or reverses a decision without knowing what it covered. |
| Technical basis | Represented state, returned results, comparators, uncertainty, mechanism limits, and implementation depth | A bounded result becomes an unqualified claim. |
| Alternatives and dissent | Rejected candidates, failed paths, unresolved objections, and reasons for the selection | Later reviewers cannot distinguish a considered choice from a missing option. |
| Rights and exceptions | Assigned roles, concurrences, permissions, waivers, expiration, and escalation paths | Authority persists after its technical basis or owner has changed. |
| Mitigation and containment | Validated fallback, disable, derating, isolation, rollback, repair, or explicit absence of a credible lever | A named containment right cannot be exercised when a failure occurs. |
| Monitoring and reopening | Signals, thresholds, version mapping, response owner, revalidation triggers, and retirement condition | Changed workloads, software, tools, or field behavior leave a stale decision in force. |

: **Transfer carries the technical argument and the continuing obligation.**
The next owner must know what can invalidate the decision and possess the right
to respond. {#tbl-ownership-transfer tbl-colwidths="[22,43,35]"}

A transfer can be proportional to consequence and reversibility. A local,
reversible study needs less than a tapeout release, but it still needs enough
state for the next authorized role to understand its limits. Proprietary
access may prevent public reproduction. It does not excuse an internal
transfer from identifying what only a protected reviewer could inspect.

Consider an explicitly composite example rather than a documented incident. A
thermal predictor is trained and calibrated with aggressive clock gating
enabled across the system, then transferred to a physical-design team for
macro placement. The model artifact arrives, but the clock-gating assumption
and its validated workload envelope do not. The new team treats its predictions
as worst-case coverage, places macros more tightly, and the resulting design
throttles under a field workload outside that envelope. The file transfer
succeeded while the technical basis failed to travel. A responsible transfer
therefore carries the conditions that make a model or result valid, not just
the model, report, or candidate.

### When a Field Result Reopens the Decision

Deployment does not end architecture responsibility. When observed behavior
exceeds ordinary variation, a named role must declare the affected product
scope and use a validated containment lever where one exists. The organization
must investigate the cause, coordinate disclosure under the applicable product
obligations, and reopen the architecture claims and exceptions that the field
result challenges. The resulting action may repair, derate, replace, or retire
the capability.

Failing silicon is high-fidelity evidence that a failure occurred under the
observed conditions. It is not automatically the root cause. The incident
study must still distinguish workload, software, hardware, package,
manufacturing, environmental, and operational explanations.

The Pentium FDIV case discussed in @sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive shows how
a small design omission can become expensive after shipment. The public record
supports missing lookup-table entries and inadequate test coverage. It does
not reconstruct every internal handoff. The durable ownership question is
which role could stop release, who owned customer response, and what evidence
would have reopened the decision before or after the failure became public.

## The Lighthouse Commitment Record

The final decision can now be stated without pretending that the missing work
was completed. @tbl-lighthouse-commitment closes the current freeze request.

| **Decision field** | **Current Lighthouse record** |
| --- | --- |
| Assessment received | The implementation-facing architecture outcome, incremental AI contribution, and moonshot program status are unresolved in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. |
| Decision scope | The request retains the XRBench-class real-time mobile XR workload, 64-bit RISC-V hardware-software basis, 3\ W subsystem target, and 3\ nm-class low-power mobile process. A later packet must pin the selected process design kit, libraries, and process, voltage, and temperature conditions. |
| Action | Refuse the current freeze of the 32 by 32 array and its software-facing interface. Retain 32 by 32 only as a reference candidate and continue the bounded implementation-readiness study. |
| Decision authority | The authorized architecture or product review authority owns the current refusal and any later freeze decision. The system architecture role owns the recommendation and request, with required concurrence from workload and software, RTL and verification, physical and power, security and reliability, and product roles. |
| Technical reason | Representative workloads, compiler and runtime behavior, mapping, interface and memory cost, subsystem energy and power, RTL behavior, physical implementation, security, owner capacity, and validated containment remain incomplete. |
| Residual-risk decision | None of these missing obligations is accepted as residual risk for an interface or RTL freeze. They remain blocking unknowns. |
| Mitigation | Test representative workloads through the compiler, runtime, mapping, and interface path. Measure the complete performance, memory, interface, energy, and 3\ W boundary. Complete the declared RTL, verification, physical, timing, power-delivery, thermal, security, and reliability checks, then verify owner capacity and required containment. Preserve per-condition results, costs, failures, and predeclared acceptance limits. Complete the credible matched comparison separately to update the AI program status. |
| Containment | Keep the candidate and interface versioned and reversible, prevent downstream dependencies from treating them as frozen, and grant no signoff or tapeout authority from the current record. No field containment claim is made before a design is selected and its levers are validated. |
| Monitoring | Track new workload, software, interface, memory, energy, implementation, security, and tool results against the same candidate and condition identities. |
| Reopening | Reopen the freeze decision when the required workload coverage, system-boundary measurements, implementation checks, owner capacity, and containment plan are complete, or earlier if a changed product condition makes the current candidate or question obsolete. Update the AI program status independently when the matched comparison is complete. |
| Expiration and dissent | This refusal remains in force until the authorized architecture or product review authority issues a superseding decision. Accepting a materially new packet only reopens review. Rejected alternatives, unresolved objections, and any minority recommendation remain attached to that packet. |

: **The current action is refusal of the freeze, not rejection of the
candidate.** Missing implementation evidence and an unresolved program
assessment remain visible rather than being converted into permission.
{#tbl-lighthouse-commitment tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

The current decision creates authorized work without authorizing commitment.
The study system may propose, screen, and evaluate candidates within the
declared budget. Domain owners may reject candidates in their assigned scopes.
The system architecture role may prepare a new recommendation. No role may
claim that AI improved the program, freeze the interface, waive the entire
missing implementation record, or infer signoff and tapeout permission from
the local simulator result.

The commitment record now carries the four groups that block reconsideration:
workload and software coverage, complete-system cost and the 3\ W boundary, RTL
and physical feasibility, and exercisable ownership and containment. These
unknowns do not become residual risk merely because the schedule wants a
decision. Their named owners, acceptance limits, and reopening conditions keep
them attached to the freeze request.

## Open Research Questions

**How can organizations test owner capacity as automated work volume grows?**
A useful test must measure authority, access, technical competence, review
time, and ability to intervene on the actions actually assigned.

**How should an architecture commitment treat opaque external dependencies?**
Vendor models, licensed IP, process information, and tools can limit
inspection and diagnosis, while responsibility, contracts, and regulation
remain distributed across organizations.

**How much direct practice preserves cross-layer judgment after routine work
is automated?** The field needs evidence about which experiences build the
ability to find missing constraints and challenge apparently clean results.

**How should the value of containment be priced before the failure is known?**
Disable paths, isolation, redundancy, derating, rollback, and repair options
consume design resources now in exchange for reversibility under an uncertain
future failure.

## Closing the Moonshot

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Architecture judgment does not begin where automation ends"}
AI can perform substantial formulation, exploration, implementation, and
analysis. Architects still choose the problem, abstraction, boundary,
cross-layer tradeoff, and consequence that determine whether the resulting
design should be committed.
:::

The two outcomes return separately to @sec-moonshot
(@tbl-lighthouse-closing-tests).

| **Closing test** | **Current outcome** | **Meaning** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AI program test | Unresolved | No adequate matched complete-system comparison yet shows that AI improves the architecture result, lowers total cost at comparable quality, or both across the required envelope. |
| Architecture commitment | Refuse the current freeze | The implementation-facing evidence does not support freezing the array and interface. The reference candidate remains open for further study. |

: **Neither closing result rescues the other.** The architecture can later be
committed even if the AI program is unsupported, and a supported AI program
can still produce an architecture that should be refused.
{#tbl-lighthouse-closing-tests tbl-colwidths="[24,25,51]"}

Three statements form the ending. The AI program status is unresolved because
the matched complete-system comparison has not been run. The current
array-and-interface freeze is refused because the implementation-facing
evidence is incomplete. The full Lighthouse moonshot remains open because
neither outcome rejects the reference candidate or establishes that the
program has failed.

This is a real ending. A refusal to cross a difficult-to-reverse boundary is an
architecture decision. It preserves the candidate, names the missing work,
assigns the rights needed to perform it, and states exactly what can reopen the
question. The review may reopen after the implementation obligations are met
or earlier when a changed product condition makes the candidate or the
architecture question obsolete. The refusal remains in force until the
authorized architecture or product review body issues a superseding decision.

The architect is not merely the person who signs after the technical work is
finished. The architecture role defines and reframes the problem, chooses
abstractions, keeps system boundaries honest, exposes missing constraints,
composes specialist judgments, distinguishes result from mechanism, and
decides what residual uncertainty means for the product. Models, methods, and
tools can contribute throughout that work without owning the final action.

Responsibility becomes concrete through rights. Proposal, execution,
acceptance, rejection, waiver, commitment, signoff, monitoring, containment,
and reopening belong to explicit roles with real authority and capacity. A
signature without access, expertise, time, or an intervention path is not
ownership. A containment right without a validated technical lever is not
containment.

If a later assessment supports the AI program, the architect must still decide
whether the selected design and its residual risks justify commitment. If a
later assessment finds no AI contribution, the same architecture may still
advance through a conventional workflow. If the assessment remains
unresolved, no one may turn the absence of a verdict into a success claim.

Architecture 2.0 is a way to use AI for system-and-chip design without reducing
architecture to model output or preserving human work merely because it was
once manual. AI extends the technical work that can be attempted. Architects
and their organizations remain responsible for deciding which problem is
worth solving, which design is worth committing, what could make that decision
wrong, and what they will do when conditions change.
